Station B — Counselling

items.text: Understanding of cervical cancer screening and the role of HPV.
Recognition of normal and abnormal cytology terminology.
Ability to distinguish low-grade from high-grade abnormalities.
Knowledge of colposcopy, cervical biopsy and follow-up.
Appropriate counselling without causing unnecessary anxiety.
Awareness that screening results are not, by themselves, a definitive diagnosis of cervical cancer.

blocks.text: If the station involves taking a cervical sample, treat it as an intimate examination and obtain informed consent.
A suitable opening statement is:

“Good morning. My name is … I understand that you have been asked to have a cervical screening test. I would like to explain the procedure, answer any questions you may have, and obtain your consent before we proceed.”

items.text: Confirm the patient's identity using appropriate identifiers.
Explain that the test collects cells from the cervix to screen for precancerous changes.
Explain the procedure, including the use of a speculum.
Ask about current vaginal bleeding, unusual discharge, pelvic pain and relevant symptoms.
Ask about previous cervical screening results, colposcopy or cervical treatment.
Establish the last menstrual period and pregnancy status where relevant.
Explain possible temporary discomfort or light spotting.
Obtain explicit consent and offer a chaperone.
Ensure privacy, appropriate draping and a comfortable position.
Explain that the patient can ask to pause or stop the procedure at any time.

blocks.text: Important distinction: Cervical screening is intended for people without symptoms. A patient with unexplained postcoital bleeding, persistent abnormal vaginal bleeding or a suspicious-looking cervix requires clinical assessment even if the screening result is normal.

blocks.text: Screening can often be performed at different points in the menstrual cycle, although heavy menstrual bleeding can interfere with sample interpretation. Follow the local laboratory's instructions about timing, lubricant use and preparation.
Avoid assuming that every screening programme uses the same sampling device, interval or follow-up algorithm.

content_groups.group_title: A. How to obtain a cervical cytology sample

blocks.text: Step 1 — Visualise the cervix

Gently insert the speculum and visualise the cervix and external os. Note any ulceration, bleeding, discharge, friability or visible mass. A suspicious lesion needs assessment regardless of the screening result.
Step 2 — Collect the sample

Insert the appropriate sampling device into contact with the transformation zone and sample according to the manufacturer's instructions. Use the specified device and technique for the local laboratory system.
Step 3 — Preserve the specimen
For liquid-based cytology, rinse or place the brush in the collection vial as instructed. For conventional cytology, spread the sample on a slide and fix it promptly.
Step 4 — Label and send
Confirm patient identifiers, complete the laboratory request form, document the procedure and send the specimen according to local protocols.

content_groups.group_title: B. Understand the Bethesda reporting system

blocks.text: The Bethesda system standardises cervical cytology reports. The key exam skill is recognising the exact abnormality and distinguishing a screening result from a histological diagnosis.

rows: Minor atypical squamous changes of uncertain significance
HPV testing or repeat testing according to the programme
A high-grade lesion cannot be excluded
Low-grade squamous abnormality, often associated with HPV
Risk-based follow-up; colposcopy depends on context
Prompt colposcopy, biopsy or appropriate expedited management

Specialist assessment and diagnostic excision are usually required

Exam pearl: CIN1, CIN2 and CIN3 are histological diagnoses made from tissue, usually a cervical biopsy. LSIL and HSIL are cytological categories. Although they are related, they are not interchangeable.
A normal cervical cytology report may read:
REPRESENTATIVE LABORATORY REPORT
Specimen adequacy: Satisfactory for evaluation.
Transformation zone component: Present.
Interpretation: Negative for intraepithelial lesion or malignancy (NILM).
Additional findings: No significant abnormality identified.

items.text: The sample is adequate for interpretation.
No cytological evidence of cervical precancer or malignancy is identified.
The presence of a transformation-zone component can support sample adequacy, but its absence does not automatically make every sample unsatisfactory.
The patient should return at the interval recommended by the relevant screening programme, taking account of HPV results and previous screening history.

blocks.text: A normal cytology result does not exclude every cervical lesion, and it does not override symptoms or a suspicious examination finding.
bethesda.soc.wisc.edu
Low-grade or indeterminate abnormality
Report: Satisfactory specimen; ASC-US.
Interpretation: Some squamous cells appear atypical, but the changes are insufficient to classify them as a definite squamous intraepithelial lesion.

Next step: Determine high-risk HPV status if the screening pathway uses HPV triage. If HPV testing is negative, surveillance may be appropriate; if positive, colposcopy or other risk-based follow-up may be indicated. Age, previous results and local protocols influence the decision.
Counselling point: ASC-US does not mean cervical cancer. It means that the cells look slightly unusual and require appropriate follow-up.
screening.iarc.fr
Low-grade lesion
Report: LSIL.
Interpretation: Cytological changes are compatible with a low-grade squamous lesion, frequently associated with HPV infection.
Next step: Use the applicable screening algorithm to decide between surveillance and colposcopy. Consider the patient's age, HPV result, previous abnormalities and risk profile.
Many low-grade HPV-associated abnormalities regress, particularly in younger patients. However, follow-up remains important.
screening.iarc.fr
High-grade abnormality
Report: HSIL.
Interpretation: Cytological features raise significant concern for a high-grade precancerous squamous lesion.

Next step: Arrange prompt colposcopic assessment and biopsy, or follow an approved risk-based pathway that may permit expedited excisional treatment in selected non-pregnant patients. Histology establishes the diagnosis when biopsy is performed.
Do not say: “The patient definitely has cervical cancer.”
Instead say:

“This is a high-grade cytological abnormality associated with a significant risk of cervical precancer. Further assessment is required to determine the underlying histology and exclude invasive disease.”
Report: ASC-H.
Interpretation: Atypical squamous cells are present, and a high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion cannot be excluded.
Management: Colposcopy with appropriate biopsy is generally indicated. A negative HPV result does not automatically eliminate the need for assessment.
Report: Atypical glandular cells (AGC).

Interpretation: Abnormal glandular cells have been identified. The differential includes benign reactive changes, cervical glandular precancer and, less commonly, invasive malignancy or endometrial pathology.
Management: Colposcopy and endocervical evaluation are usually required. Endometrial sampling may also be indicated depending on age, bleeding symptoms and endometrial cancer risk factors.
Report: Endocervical adenocarcinoma in situ.
Interpretation: A glandular precancerous lesion is suspected.

Management: Refer for specialist assessment and diagnostic excision to establish the extent of disease and exclude invasion. Subsequent management depends on histology, excision margins, fertility wishes and whether conservative treatment is appropriate.

content_groups.group_title: Case 7: Cytology suspicious for squamous cell carcinoma

blocks.text: Report: Cytological features suspicious for squamous cell carcinoma.
Interpretation: Malignant disease is suspected; screening alone cannot establish the full diagnosis or stage.
Management: Urgent gynaecological oncology referral, examination and tissue biopsy. Additional imaging is used when indicated for staging after the diagnostic assessment.
Report: Unsatisfactory for evaluation because of scant cellularity or obscuring blood/inflammation.
Interpretation: The laboratory cannot reliably determine whether abnormal cells are present.

Management: Repeat sampling according to the relevant screening guideline, taking account of the reason for inadequacy. If the patient has symptoms or a suspicious cervix, investigate those findings without waiting for routine repeat screening.

content_groups.group_title: Case 9: High-risk HPV positive, cytology negative

blocks.text: Report: High-risk HPV detected; cytology NILM.
Interpretation: A carcinogenic HPV type is detected, but no cytological precancerous lesion is identified in the sample.

Management: Use HPV genotyping, previous results and the local risk-based algorithm to determine whether colposcopy or repeat HPV-based testing is appropriate. HPV16 or HPV18 positivity commonly warrants more intensive assessment.

content_groups.group_title: Case 10: Cytology negative but the cervix looks suspicious

blocks.text: Clinical scenario: A woman reports recurrent postcoital bleeding. Cervical cytology is NILM, but examination reveals a friable cervical lesion.
Interpretation: The clinical findings take priority over reassurance from the screening result.
Management: Arrange urgent gynaecological assessment and biopsy of the suspicious lesion. Do not simply repeat cytology or wait for the next screening interval.

subsections.subsection_title: 7. How to report cervical cytology findings

blocks.text: In an OSCE, use a systematic format rather than simply stating “the smear is abnormal.”

items.text: S — Specimen adequacy.
A — Additional findings.
I — Interpretation or general categorisation.
C — Cytological diagnosis.
N — Next clinical step.

blocks.text: **Report 1 — Normal cytology**

“The specimen is satisfactory for evaluation. The cytological interpretation is negative for intraepithelial lesion or malignancy. No significant cytological abnormality is identified. I would correlate with the HPV result and arrange routine screening according to the applicable programme.”

“The specimen is satisfactory and demonstrates a low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion, commonly associated with HPV infection. This is an abnormal screening result but does not establish the presence of invasive cancer. I would review the HPV status, previous screening history and applicable risk-based pathway to determine the need for surveillance or colposcopy.”

“The specimen is satisfactory and demonstrates a high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion. This raises significant concern for cervical precancer, including possible CIN2 or CIN3 on histology. I would arrange prompt colposcopic assessment and appropriate biopsy or management through an approved high-grade lesion pathway.”

“The specimen is inadequate for reliable interpretation, so a negative result cannot be assigned. I would arrange repeat sampling according to the relevant guideline and investigate any concerning symptoms or examination findings independently.”
When an abnormal cervical cytology report is presented, the differential depends on the cellular changes and clinical context.

rows: Transient HPV infection, inflammation, atrophy or reactive changes
HPV-associated infection or low-grade squamous lesion
High-grade cervical intraepithelial neoplasia, particularly CIN2 or CIN3
Reactive glandular changes, cervical glandular precancer, endometrial pathology or malignancy
Invasive cervical malignancy or, depending on cell type, another malignancy
Low cellularity, obscuring blood, inflammation or technical sampling problems

blocks.text: Important: Cytology cannot reliably distinguish all these possibilities. Colposcopy, biopsy and other investigations establish the diagnosis where indicated.

content_groups.group_title: A. Investigations following an abnormal screening result

blocks.text: 1. High-risk HPV testing
Detects carcinogenic HPV types. Genotyping, particularly for HPV16 and HPV18, can help determine the next step in management.
2. Colposcopy
Magnified examination of the cervix, usually using acetic acid and sometimes iodine, to identify abnormal areas for further assessment.
3. Cervical biopsy
Histological examination determines whether CIN or invasive cancer is present. The histological grade guides subsequent management.
4. Endocervical assessment
Endocervical sampling may be indicated when glandular abnormalities are suspected or the transformation zone cannot be fully assessed, depending on the clinical circumstances.

items.text: Endometrial biopsy: For selected patients with AGC, abnormal uterine bleeding or risk factors for endometrial disease.
Excisional biopsy: Such as large loop excision of the transformation zone (LLETZ), to obtain tissue for diagnosis and sometimes treatment.
HIV testing: Offer according to national testing guidance and clinical context; HIV status affects cervical screening and follow-up recommendations.

Imaging: MRI, CT or other appropriate imaging may be required if invasive malignancy is diagnosed or strongly suspected, particularly for staging. Imaging is not routinely required for an isolated minor cytological abnormality.

blocks.text: The WHO recommends HPV-based screening as the preferred primary screening approach where available and recommends structured follow-up after positive results.
NCBI Bookshelf
Management is guided by the precise cytology result, HPV status, age, pregnancy, previous screening results, clinical symptoms and the national screening programme.

rows: Routine screening at the recommended interval
HPV triage or repeat testing, depending on the pathway
Prompt colposcopy, biopsy or approved expedited treatment in selected patients
Colposcopy and endocervical assessment; consider endometrial sampling when indicated
Urgent referral for tissue diagnosis and staging

blocks.text: These are general principles, not a substitute for the exact local management algorithm.

Pregnancy

items.text: Abnormal cytology should be assessed according to pregnancy-specific guidance.
Colposcopy and a clinically indicated biopsy may be performed when appropriate.
Endocervical curettage is contraindicated in pregnancy.
Treatment of precancerous lesions is generally deferred until after pregnancy unless invasive cancer is suspected and requires further evaluation.

blocks.text: Desire for future fertility

Discuss the reproductive implications of excisional treatment, particularly when repeated or deep cervical excisions are being considered. Management should balance the risk of persistent or progressive disease against the potential obstetric consequences of treatment.
Immunocompromised patients

Patients living with HIV and some other immunocompromised patients have a higher risk of persistent HPV infection and cervical disease. They may need earlier screening and more intensive follow-up according to the applicable guideline.

content_groups.group_title: C. Counselling a patient with an abnormal result

items.text: Explain the result: Use the exact report terminology.
Reassure appropriately: An abnormal smear does not automatically mean cancer.
Explain HPV: It is a common infection; a positive result does not establish when it was acquired or imply recent infidelity.
Explain the next step: HPV triage, repeat testing, colposcopy or biopsy as indicated.
Emphasise follow-up: Ensure the patient knows when and where to attend.
Address concerns: Ask about anxiety, fertility plans and questions.
Safety-net: Advise assessment for persistent postcoital bleeding, unexplained vaginal bleeding, persistent abnormal discharge or other concerning symptoms.

subsections.subsection_title: 12. Model answers for common viva scenarios

content_groups.group_title: Scenario A: A 29-year-old patient has ASC-US

blocks.text: Examiner: What would you tell her?
Model answer:

“Your screening test has shown some mildly atypical cervical cells. This does not mean that you have cervical cancer. These changes can be associated with HPV infection and may resolve. I would check whether high-risk HPV testing is available and review your previous screening results to determine whether repeat testing or colposcopy is appropriate. It is important that you attend the recommended follow-up.”

content_groups.group_title: Scenario B: A patient has HSIL

blocks.text: Examiner: What is your next step?
Model answer:

“I would explain that the result is a high-grade abnormality associated with an increased risk of significant cervical precancer. I would arrange prompt colposcopy and appropriate biopsy, or follow an approved expedited management pathway if she meets the criteria. I would review pregnancy status, reproductive plans and previous screening history, and ensure that follow-up is documented.”

content_groups.group_title: Scenario C: The cervix is visibly malignant but cytology is normal

blocks.text: Examiner: Would you repeat the smear?
Model answer:

“No. A suspicious visible cervical lesion requires urgent gynaecological assessment and tissue biopsy. A normal cytology result does not exclude invasive disease, and repeating screening alone could delay diagnosis.”
Calling HSIL cervical cancer
HSIL is a high-grade cytological abnormality. It is not synonymous with invasive malignancy.
Confusing LSIL with CIN1
LSIL is a cytology category; CIN1 is a histological diagnosis. They are related but not interchangeable.
Ignoring HPV status
HPV results, genotyping and previous screening history may substantially change the next step.
Reassuring a patient with a suspicious cervix because cytology is normal
Symptoms and examination findings must be investigated independently.
Forgetting consent during sampling
Cervical sampling requires explanation, consent, privacy, appropriate infection prevention and a sensitive approach.
Treating every abnormal result identically
ASC-US, LSIL, HSIL, AGC and AIS have different implications and require different pathways.
